text.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's whole program as an answer to a plain question: if the Torah says keeping it is 'very close', why do most people find it hard? The sefer exists to make that closeness understood.

An oath the soul does not remember still works: it leaves an impression that subconsciously gives courage and drive, the way Avraham's oath would give Eliezer strength against second thoughts on his mission.

Through the interchange of beis and pei, shevuah is linked to shefa, so the oath itself is a flow of strength from above; he shows that a written pei holds a white beis within it, a pei being a fortified beis.
The word mashpia is tied to meshupa, slanted: just as rain flows down only from a slanted roof, as for a mikveh, influence from above reaches a person only along an incline.
Because man contains all of creation, an oath binds every part of him; this is why even one suspected about money is not suspected about an oath, since an oath leaves no hidden exit.
In lashon hakodesh the name reveals the purpose: a shulchan is so called because its bounty is 'sent' to each person individually from Hashem, as fuel for his own mission.

The Mashgiach compares the Rosh Hashanah categories to the 'tzaddik' and 'rasha' of a din Torah: the one who wins a case is called the tzaddik for that case, though in other ways he may be a complete rasha, so the labels describe the judgment, not the person.
He pictures every person as standing before a court of three judges: the yetzer tov and yetzer hara each issue a ruling in the heart, and Hashem gives the verdict.
He reads 'chalal' in David HaMelech's words as 'empty': the left chamber of the heart, the seat of the yetzer hara, stood spiritually empty, just as a corpse emptied of its soul is called a chalal.
According to the Mashgiach, people do not remember their earlier gilgulim because the memory would remove their free choice; great tzaddikim, who have no free choice anyway, do remember.

He explains the four klipos with a walnut: three shells are peeled away, but the thin skin on the kernel is eaten with it and becomes part of the nut, which is klipas nogah, the shell that can be raised to holiness.
He finds the same four layers in the milah: three layers are cut away, while the fourth, the priah, is not cut but pushed back, corresponding to nogah.
The Mashgiach reads Yaakov's seven years 'like a few days' as proof of spiritual love: physical longing makes each day a year, while love for holiness, like building a sukkah, makes years fly.
Yaakov's kiss of Rachel is compared to a tzaddik kissing his tefillin and tzitzis, since she was for him the epitome of holiness.
A Hebrew servant loses the 'mem', the forty days in which the Torah was given, from 'mishpachah', and what remains is 'shifchah'.
Chanukah, the eighth after seven like Yovel after the Shemitos, can lift souls that even Shabbos cannot.
Yaakov's grief over Rachel was the loss of the geulah she embodied, and Migdal Eder, where Moshiach will appear, was Hashem's consolation.
The Tanya says 'mamash' of the soul being part of G-d, but 'by way of a parable' of Yisrael arising in Hashem's thought, because His thought is unlike ours.
Neshamah and neshimah share one word: breath is a person's inwardness, so Hashem blowing into Adam means His own life entered him.
The Torah does not stress middos because good middos are the entrance requirement: whoever enters the school of Torah is assumed to have graduated from the school of middos.
Da'as is responsibility: a child may out-learn adults, yet he is not a bar da'as because there is no bridge yet by which his understanding governs his middos.

Love cannot be commanded into being, just as a man cannot decide to love spinach, but fear is within one's choice; therefore yirah is the 'avodas avodah' a person works on and ahavah the 'avodas matanah' Hashem grants in return.
The intensity of the words of love by Shechem shows a spark of kedushah struggling to tear itself free of the klipah, like a bird pulling with all its strength out of a trap.
The love born of Binah is the fire in the heart thirsting for water, and that water is Chochmah, the point of G-dliness in the soul: the love yearns to return to its own source.
The Tanya calls love without Da'as 'dimyonos shav', not 'sheker': shav means there is something there, only it is useless, and later chapters say it has some worth.
The Mashgiach calls Gehinnom a laundry: it washes off the stain of a sin committed against a mitzvah once kept, but it cannot supply a mitzvah that was never done at all.
He says people avoid the depths of Torah because understanding more makes them more responsible, and that one who accepts pshat, remez and drush without sod is a 'pered', a mule.
How high a person can reach in Torah depends on how high the roots of his soul reach, as in an inverted tree whose roots are in heaven; even the Beis Yosef fell asleep at the Arizal's shiurim on sod.
A positive commandment overrides a prohibition because it is active and comes from love, while fear only holds back; love is the son, fear the servant.

A human organ is called by the name of a divine attribute because it is a receiver for it: the eye is an 'ayin' because Hashem's seeing is drawn into it, and when guarded according to the Torah it becomes a chariot for that holiness.
The Mashgiach reads the Midrash of the heartless donkey together with 'kaved lev Paroh': a heart that does not fear Hashem is not a heart at all, only a liver.
Fear of punishment is really fear for oneself; true fear of Hashem is the natural shame one feels before greatness, as no one would act disgracefully in front of a president.
Ordinarily a garment is secondary to its wearer, but the garments of Torah and mitzvos are greater than the soul they clothe, because Torah is not a product of Hashem's wisdom but G-dliness itself.

The Mashgiach reads chalitzah through the soul: the soul in the body is like a foot in a shoe, only its lowest part, while the rest stays above as an encompassing light, and the more refined a person is, the more of it he draws in.

The Tanya's claim that the garments surpass the soul refers to the soul as it is in the body; at its root, since Yisrael preceded everything in Hashem's thought, the soul is above Torah, and Torah is secondary to it.

The mind's failure to grasp G-dliness is a matter of category, not capacity: just as hearing a million times better will never let one hear a picture, a mind of any intelligence cannot reach what lies beyond this world.

Hashem's greatness and humility appear together: His greatness is that no mind can grasp Him, and His humility is that He contracted His will and wisdom into halachos of oxen and sukkos so that our minds can.

Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim were a chain, each mashal explaining the one above it, and in the same way Torah came down through the worlds, so that people on earth grasp it better than the angels, who lack this world's concepts.
The Mashgiach reverses the common view: the physical table one can touch belongs to the imaginary world, while Hashem's presence, which seems abstract, is the true reality.
Every detail of the halachos of sukkah, such as two walls and a tefach, is a detail of the Name of Hashem from which the mitzvah comes, so the halachos cannot be explained but only accepted.
The shaking of a Jew in learning and davening is itself part of the act of Torah and is clothed in it; it comes from the fire of the soul, which moves like a flame.
Every Jew has the potential of prophecy, since the soul knows and feels everything; only the body, insulated by aveiros, fails to pick up the soul's messages.
Learning Torah in this world is grasping Hashem Himself, like the sun itself, while the souls in Gan Eden grasp only the rays of the Shechinah.
Water, which is chesed, is the medium of every physical pleasure, and Hashem's embrace of a person reaches him through the Torah, the water that comes down from above.
A philosopher can see depth in the Tanya yet miss its point entirely, like someone without an ear for music who cannot tell a symphony from a cat walking on a piano.

Idle sitting by ten Jews is not merely wasted time: since the Shechinah is there regardless, they 'squeeze' it, like people crowding someone out of a room, and this is counted among the causes of golus.
Just as Hashem concealed His holiness in physical things through the halachos, He wrapped the deepest secrets of the Torah in even more coverings, the aggados that seem like nonsense.
The Torah is Hashem encased in physical subject matter like radioactive material in lead: the casing does not interrupt the contact, just as a caress through a sleeve is still a caress.
By learning Torah a Jew rises above the angels and the souls in Gan Eden, who receive only light that radiates from the Shechinah, while he holds the Shechinah itself.

The Gemara discusses cases that may never occur, such as a person with two heads, because each halachah is Hashem's own will about what would be if it happened, so understanding it is grasping His will.
Clothing costs more than food because mitzvos, which are clothing, should be paid for, while Torah, which is food, comes free.

The sukkah is a surrounding light and the lulav draws some of it inward; when Sukkos ends, the Torah of Simchas Torah gives an inner light, which the generation of the flood, given only an ark like a sukkah, did not merit.

The gravity of a sin and the ease of its repair are separate questions: wasted seed is the worst sin, yet because its influence found no receiver, it can be gathered back more easily than forbidden relations.
Yaakov's gift to Esav totaled 580 animals, the numerical value of Esav's force in the Sitra Achra with its female counterpart, so sending it from the side of kedushah neutralized that force.
The customs of the nations, like putting the woman first, buttoning left over right and writing left to right, follow unknowingly from their angel's left-sided order, while Jews start from the right.
The Jewish calendar blends the moon of chesed with the sun of din through the leap month, unlike the Arabs' purely lunar calendar of uncontrolled chesed, so Nisan always falls in spring.
Tumas keri is linked by the Midrash to Amalek's 'chance', so its repair, as Rav Tzadok says, is faith in Hashem's oneness, that nothing simply happens.
Following the Tzemach Tzedek, the halachah that no brachah is said on forbidden food rests on the inner purpose of a brachah: to elevate the holy sparks, which forbidden food cannot release.

The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's term 'divrei soferim' for rabbinic law as a claim about the Rabbis' vision: because single letters were 'davar shebeminyan' to them, they saw the root of things and could know that a rabbinic prohibition draws from the klipos and is not merely a fence.
Rabbi Meir's writing a Megillah by heart did not break the rule of copying from a text, because he saw the Torah's root in heaven and copied from it.

The difference between 'or' with an ayin, skin, and 'or' with an aleph, light, describes the whole avodah of a Jew: to see the aleph, the Master of the world, inside the ayin, which sweetens all impurity.

The suspended ayin of 'chazir miyaar' stands at the middle of Tehillim because the center, the point of origin, is the place where things can be changed, so even the swine, the counterpart of the serpent, can turn from ayin to aleph there.
Chalav akum can be worse than chazir: chazir is forbidden only as itself, while chalav akum carries a connection to the goy, which reaches the root of the shedim nukhraim.
Tosafos records that the old man who drank the wine was later killed in order to prove his point: had the wine truly been yayin nesech, he would not have merited to give his life al kiddush Hashem.
Food eaten for pleasure is like dust on a mattress that stays on the surface and is beaten out, while forbidden food is absorbed like a real stain that needs the hot laundering of Gehinnom.

The Gehinnom of fire answers active sins, since every action needs energy and generates heat, while the Gehinnom of snow answers the passive failure to do a mitzvah, a coldness in which no heat was generated for a mitzvah.

Idle talk about baseball comes from a passion of the middos and defiles only them, but substantive secular wisdom defiles Chabad, the soul's intellect, which is above the middos; this is why the more serious study is the greater blemish.
Secular wisdom is a kelipah precisely because it comes from very great lights: the vessels could not receive them and broke, and the fallen fragments of Chabad became this wisdom.
The wife's name given only for Hadar, the eighth king, shows that a receiver had now come into being alongside the giver, so that world could endure, unlike the seven kings of whom it says 'he died'.

The founding principle of Greek philosophy, still held by scientists, that one does not accept what one cannot understand, is not science but fear; a real scientist who delves into creation knows better than anyone that there are things he cannot understand.
Chanukah's unique mehadrin min hamehadrin, found by no other mitzvah, is tied to Hadar, the eighth king who did not die, because the wisdom of Yavan is not a total kelipah and can return to holiness.

The Breaking of the Vessels is like a hava amina in the Gemara, which holds holiness even though it is rejected: Hashem gave existence to something without substance so that the world would be one of free choice.

The animal soul is what keeps creatures, people included, alive: people do not live because they decide to, but because natural desires to eat and sleep drive them, and this is Hashem's device to keep the world going.

Rashi's description of Mitzrayim and of Yisrael at Sinai uses the same phrases in reverse order: for the yetzer hara the heart comes first and then the person, for the yetzer tov the mind comes first and then the heart.

The order of the blessings of Krias Shema mirrors the Tanya: contemplating creation and the angels' awe produces fear, then love, and only with both does one say Shema; at Ahavah Rabbah the angels are no longer mentioned, since Israel stands higher.
Anger at people who live differently usually reveals insecurity about one's own path, or pride in one's Rebbe and crowd, rather than true zeal for Heaven.
The Radbaz answers why chametz is treated so strictly with searching and destroying: chametz is the yetzer hara, and in the war against it one goes with full determination.

The source of pleasure is in the mind: true intellectual delight is what one feels solving a problem alone on an island, while rushing to tell a friend shows the pleasure is already mixed with something else.
Nullification means the limbs serve the soul the way a pen serves a writer: the pen does not argue about what to write, and a chariot has no will of its own apart from its rider.
In holiness the mind arouses the heart; in impurity the heart's desires send up their vapors and the mind becomes their servant, devising ways to satisfy them.

Ahavah rabbah is a pleasure that does not need the heart: the mind itself has a delight of understanding, like the flash of grasping a hard idea, and this is a taste of what souls enjoy in the World to Come.
Pharaoh withstood the plagues because in him the process of the tzaddik ran in reverse: the left chamber overflowed into the right, and his heart became only liver, the seat of the yetzer hara.

Man's organs are likenesses of the powers Scripture attributes to Hashem, so a rasha's heart that does not fear Hashem does not deserve to be called a heart, and his eye that does not look to Hashem is not truly an eye.

The angel of Esav picked a fight with Yaakov on the very night before his turn to sing shirah because his shirah was to be overpowered: every creature's shirah is fulfilling its function, just as the sun's shirah is its motion.

'Chalal' means empty: a person who dies is called a chalal because he is emptied of his nefesh, and chillul Shabbos means emptying Shabbos of its kedushah; so David's 'chalal' heart was empty of the yetzer hara.
The tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era were sent close to Moshiach's days, outside the normal descent of the generations, to inject Klal Yisrael with 'adrenaline' so that its heart keeps beating.

Forgetting earlier gilgulim is what makes free choice possible: whoever remembered why he was sent back would not fail to be a tzaddik; perfect tzaddikim, who live only for others, have no choice to protect and so may remember.
Even a rasha's downfall is a merit, since it brings a Kiddush Hashem; Czar Nicholas was so wicked that he was denied even that and died a natural death.

The double wording about David and Avimelech, that he was driven out and that he went, describes the yetzer hara of the incomplete tzaddik: he thinks he drove it out, but it left of its own will and is ready to attack again.

The mitzvah of matzah is achila, and achila means enjoying the eating; this is why the Apter Rav, who tasted nothing all year, would not give up the matzah of the Seder, and why on Pesach the body itself is to feel the mitzvah.
Mius, revulsion, is felt toward objects and sinah toward people; David's utmost hatred of the resha'im is the soul's revulsion at their spiritual being, as the senses are revolted by spoiled food.

The Mashgiach resolves the apparent contradiction between the 18,000 tzaddikim before Hashem and Rabbi Shimon's 'bnei aliyah are few': the 18,000 still hold a tiny dormant trace of evil, while the bnei aliyah transformed it entirely.
He reads 'chassid ha'mitchased im kono' with 'kono' as 'his nest': the true chassid does kindness with Hashem's nest, the Shechinah in the lower world, giving it a proper place to rest.

Even the desire for closeness to Hashem, if served for its own sake, still points to the self; the ben aliyah has that thirst but does his mitzvos only for Hashem, since any act for himself would mean ego and a separation from Him.

The Sitra Achra can snatch a destined union only temporarily; the Mashgiach sees this pattern in a person's match, in Eretz Yisrael first held by Canaan, and in Bathsheba first married to another before coming to David.
Because the Satan tries to block Moshiach's coming, everything leading to Moshiach comes about in a hidden, roundabout way, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can so the thief will not look there.

A thought of sin can be worse than the deed because thought reaches the higher world where speech and action cannot, like a small grease spot that is nothing on the avenue but an offense in the king's palace.
Every person has a deep chamber in his heart that is a tzaddik gamur, and when he says 'l'shem yichud' that chamber means it with all that it implies.

The Midrash's piece of Torah from the am ha'aretz, that Esav will return Yaakov's animals to Moshiach, was his own portion in the Torah: the souls given over to Esav, like him, will ultimately return to Yaakov and become tzaddikim.
Just as the tzaddik never even thinks of sinning, the rasha v'ra lo is his exact counterpart who never even thinks of teshuvah.

The surplus half-shekels of the Jews beyond six hundred thousand became the silver hooks that protruded outside the holiness of the Mishkan; Haman did not bother to counter them, thinking those outcast Jews mattered to no one, and that was his mistake.

The thirteenth month has no combination of the four letters of Hashem's Name, which allow only twelve, so it stands outside the camp; the Purim miracle happening in Adar Sheni shows it was made for the Jews outside the camp.
Korach's flaw of division reached Yitzhar, Kehas and Levi but could not reach Yisrael, because the Yechidah that unites all of Klal Yisrael is untouchable.

Ordinary Purim is for the rasha v'tov lo who still has regret, while Shushan Purim of Yerushalayim, the walled city surrounded like a makif, is a higher level, for those who have nothing within themselves but the makif.
The Mashgiach stresses that the Tanya's beinoni, who never sins even in thought, is what we would call a virtual tzaddik; he is called a beinoni only because the potential for sin still lives in him.
He reads the beinoni's 'never will sin' like the Rambam's testimony of the One Who knows hidden things about a baal teshuvah: it describes how resolute he is now, not a guarantee about the future.
With an analogy of antibiotics stopped too early, he explains that the beinoni's yetzer hara is knocked out like dormant microbes that can revive, whereas the tzaddik's is dead.
He explains that since Above there is no time, the eis ratzon formed at sunrise in Eretz Yisrael travels with the sunrise, so each place has the original eis ratzon in its own morning.
He describes the air up to Shamayim as full of klipos from people's sins, so Pesukei Dezimra must cut a channel through them, matching the Arizal's reading of 'zimra' as cutting.
He compares the beinoni in davening to a Chassid dancing on Shabbos: he rises above his normal height but lands again, while the tzaddik truly stands that high.
He says an intruding thought is an opportunity: a person was sent down to wage this war, and if the enemy never came he could never fight it.

Man, like the world created with ten utterances in four letters, has forty powers; sin involves only thirty-nine, which is why the Sages read 'forty lashes' as thirty-nine: the fortieth level, the 'tip of the yud', is never touched by sin.
The atonement of Yom Kippur, 'before Hashem', comes from above the yud of Hashem's Name, the Holy of Holies within the Jew, where sin never entered.
Amalek is the 'first' of impurity, its own 'tip of the yud', set against the innermost point of holiness; Esther feared he had penetrated even there.
Mordechai is called 'ben Kish' because he knocked on the gates of mercy, opening the Holy of Holies on an ordinary day; a tzaddik's great act affects all Jewish souls.
The Tanya omits avak lashon hara from the three daily sins because a thought can be repelled before it is a sin, but words once spoken are already a sin, and a Beinoni does not speak them.
In holiness the mind gives birth to love and fear in the heart; in impurity desire rises from the heart to the mind, and if not allowed to linger it gives birth to nothing and dissipates.
The Mashgiach cites his father-in-law: Yosef told his brothers that their enmity was arranged by Heaven to test whether he would bear a grudge, so it was through their merit that he passed the test.
Loving one Jew more than another is only from the side of the body; from the side of the soul all Jews are one soul, so love of Israel does not divide the love of Hashem.
The word titharu equals keser in gematria, and the goral, like the skull above the brain, is above understanding; both Yom Kippur and Purim come through a goral and reach keser.
Shema, with its enlarged ayin, equals keser in gematria, which is why Haman, drawing on the keser of impurity, wanted to stop Mordechai from saying Shema.
Haman is called tzorer haYehudim because tzorer means to bind: by threatening them he caused the Jews to unite against him.
Just as an eiruv makes several families one household through shared food, mishloach manos on Purim makes all of Klal Yisrael one table.

Yosef pressed his brothers so that their suffering would finish the repair of his sale; had he held back a few more moments the repair would have been complete, and the Torah's words that he could not restrain himself are a lament.
The Tanya says 'like a rasha' and not 'a rasha' because the beinoni is not wicked; he only carries the full potential to become one if he is not on guard.

Sometimes it is precisely the sin and its damage that reveals Hashem's hidden love, as a child's broken leg turns the father from discipline to mercy; this is why Moshe stressed that the sin of the Calf was great.
At the very party where the Jews sinned by joining Achashverosh's celebration, Hashem was already preparing their salvation through Vashti's removal, showing a father's love even in the worst state.
The worse concealment is not when the father hides but when the child does not even know he is there; the work of Adar is to reveal the hiding.
Adar Sheni has no combination of the four-letter name of its own, since only twelve are possible, so its concealment is greater, and for that reason the Purim miracle in it was greater.
A stronger urge to sin need not mean a fall: it may come because the beinoni was raised to a higher level and must pass a test to show he is worthy of it.

Nefesh in mesiras nefesh means one's will, so giving up a small desire each day is itself mesiras nefesh, and Hashem counts the sum total, while people judge only the single blow, like grains of a ground-up stone.
The beinoni is a tzaddik in one chamber of his heart: there, where his hidden love of Hashem lives, he truly hates evil.

A person is built of forty levels, and the sinner receives thirty-nine lashes rather than forty because his fortieth level never sinned; on Yom Kippur, the fortieth day of teshuvah, that level surfaces and every Jew is forgiven.

Wisdom, Torah and Hashem give different answers about the sinner not as contradictions but as rising levels, and at the highest Hashem judges by the inner will of a Jew, who truly wants to do His will.
A bad thought that enters the mind is not a sin but a privilege, an opportunity; the sin is only in letting it linger and exploring it.
The greatest mitzvah ever done, the Akeidah, was performed by Avraham Avinu with his levels taken from him and without feeling; this is why it is the merit invoked whenever Jews need a zechus.
A special warm tefillah or elation during a mitzvah may be the reward for an earlier hard-won victory over the yetzer, even a day or a year before.

Whether a soul is drawn to Torah or to tefillah depends on whether it was rooted in the head or the heart of Adam Harishon; one who misuses that root may become a scientist or a philosopher, or a poet or songwriter.
Like a tuning fork that sets matching piano strings vibrating, the beinoni's effort to act like a tzaddik sets the corresponding heavenly chords vibrating and draws down a tzaddik's soul.
The Tanya deliberately calls the beinoni's trained joy truth according to his level rather than absolute truth, since each person has his own level of truth.
Even when an ibbur departs, it leaves a residue of kedushah in the soul and a memory that spurs the person to try to reach that level again.

The Mashgiach reads the difference between 'oved' and 'eved' grammatically: 'oved' is a present participle, a man still in the act of serving, while 'eved' is a title earned, as 'ganav' names one who has actually stolen and not one able to steal.

The same yetzer hara that caused the Flood became the reason not to bring another, because the generations before it were giants held fully responsible, while the world after it is like a sick child who is left alone.
A good routine can itself mean one is not serving Hashem: one who reached the level of masmid through struggle stops being an 'oved Elokim' once it becomes second nature, unless he pushes beyond it.

A hundred reviews stay within the domain of the yetzer hara, whose name has the gematria of a hundred, while the hundred and first moves into the domain of the angel Michael, whose name equals a hundred and one, where forgetting no longer rules.
Even a natural masmid with no struggle in quantity can become an 'oved Elokim' through quality, learning better, where there is no limit to growth.
A Jew's emunah is a hereditary knowledge, like the beaver that builds a dam with an engineer's skill though separated from its mother at birth.
Avraham and Sarah were barren because Avraham was a new species cut off from the earlier generations; the hei added to his name was a new power of birth, and with him creation was completed.
The greater a tzaddik's understanding, the more he sees that Hashem is greater still; emunah begins exactly where his understanding stops.

Milah is done at eight days, before the child has understanding, because it is the sign of emunah above daas; Yishmael's milah waits for thirteen because it is like any mitzvah that needs daas, an empty milah.
Every tzaddik has his adversary: Avraham had Nimrod, Yitzchak had Yishmael and Yaakov had Esav; the end of the exile comes through the fall of Yishmael before Yitzchak.
Milah is the most striking defiance of nature: as soon as a child is born one cuts off what nature produced, declaring that this is not how a Jew is made.

The Mashgiach compares a soul's development to conception, pregnancy, birth and nursing: a soul sent down before its 'birth' has not yet come into the world, so it cannot give out felt love however much it contemplates.
He shows 'ratzo vashov' as the pattern of all creation: day and night, summer and winter, and the pulse that pushes blood up and lets it fall back until the next beat.

Citing a sefer, he explains that Avraham's words 'we will return' at the Akeidah kept his soul from leaving him in his great dveikus, while Sarah, hearing that her son had been ready to give his life, was so charged with love that her soul left her.
He explains that in galus the tzaddikim long for Hashem more than in the days of the Beis HaMikdash, as a man in the desert without water thirsts more than one who has water at hand.

The Mashgiach applies the Gemara's rule that a shliach can only do what the sender can do: the heart can be the limbs' shliach because it is physical like them, while the mind, being higher, is not a fitting shliach.
He explains that since the Ba'al HaTanya holds that all Torah and mitzvos must come from contemplation of Hashem's greatness, Chabad Chassidim learn so much Chassidus that speaks of that greatness.

He links 'Hashem combines it with the deed' to the Rema on 'u'mafli la'asos': just as Hashem wondrously joins the spiritual soul to the physical body, He joins the mind's love to the physical mitzvah.
The Mashgiach reads 'ki karov' as speaking to every generation and every moment, rejecting the idea that it was meant only for the great souls of Moshe Rabbeinu's generation.

The Mashgiach rejects 'sublimating' worldly enjoyment as a way to claim complete love of Hashem: thinking of the Creator while enjoying the ice cream is good, but if one enjoys it, the love is divided.
The Mashgiach explains that the Tanya does not demand abstaining from pleasure; it demands that when a mitzvah comes, the mind's recognition of duty carries the action.
The felt joy of a mitzvah is its reward, which tzaddikim taste even in this world; it is not what is asked of everyone here.
The Mashgiach suggests that the rasha's punishment after losing control follows the Gemara's principle that what starts with negligence and ends with compulsion is still culpable.
The Mashgiach links the lower teshuvah to Chanukah: the wicks and oils that cannot burn on Shabbos burn on Chanukah, since then Hashem comes down to lift even the fallen.
Like a heavy object dropped from a roof into mud, the higher a spark of kedushah, the deeper it sank; so a rasha who sank into tumah and does teshuvah raises sparks that are beyond a tzaddik's reach.
The Avos are called fathers rather than grandfathers because, unlike ordinary ancestry whose bond weakens with each generation, their bond to every Jew stays as close as a father's.

A Jew who denies Hashem resembles a man who ate something harmful and lost his appetite: the craving is not gone, the stomach is only temporarily out of order, and so too the soul poisoned by sin still holds its emunah.
The world is beriah, yesh me'ayin, but a Jewish soul is not; even though its body is created, its bond to Hashem is a direct extension, like that of a child to a father.

The Satan guards against Moshiach's birth, so the great kedushah comes hidden in places he never suspects, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can; David's ruddy appearance even made the Satan think he was his.

Habit can change a middah, as a cruel man who keeps doing chesed is changed, but the love of Hashem in a Jew is an existing entity, which is either there or not, and the Tanya teaches that it is there in everyone.
Chochmah is read as 'koach mah', a power that is a question mark: we receive its flashes but cannot know where they come from, as a watch cannot understand the watchmaker.
Tefillin are the person's Keser: part of him yet above the brain, the source from which the mind receives its flashes.
In emunah the roles flip: the 'wise man' who reasons whether to believe is the greatest fool, and the one who believes with simple faith has the greatest wisdom.

Reb Chaim Brisker's remark that a Rosh ruling without proof is firmer than one with proof, since its source is the whole of Shas that shaped his mind, explains why the Chasam Sofer could rule on the father's instinct with no proof.
Because ownership (kinyan) is in the Torah, the blueprint of creation, it is built into creation itself, so an ox knows its owner.
Yishmael's claim to greatness for undergoing milah at thirteen shows the opposite: milah is above daas, so a milah done by choice as an adult misses its point.
Wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos are fit for Chanukah: there are souls that even Shabbos does not ignite, but Chanukah, a glimpse of the light of Moshiach, can.
The flame's side-to-side flicker is its effort to tear loose from the wick, like a dentist rocking a tooth before pulling it, and the same fire in a Jew makes him sway when he learns and davens.
Because fire is rooted in the sphere of the moon, a candle burns better at night when the moon itself is present, which is why bedikas chametz is done at night.
A person who feels depressed about lacking wealth, wisdom or strength compared to others shows pride, not humility, since he feels he is something that deserves more.
In English the word 'I' is capitalized even mid-sentence, reflecting ego, whereas the Torah has no such enlarged letter for 'ani'.

Kelipah's chesed is called Kna'ani, from 'hachna'ah', submission: its giver submits to the receiving side because he really gives for himself, like a donor who wants a plaque or a darshan who speaks for pay.
In the tzaddik's case the wick is the body and the flame is the soul: the body alone holds him back from flying up to Hashem until his time comes.

Every aveirah, even a small rabbinic one, is a hidden subdivision of avodah zarah, because it throws a person under the jurisdiction of the sitra achra, the same domain as idolatry, only not its 'top' form.

A Jew's readiness to die rather than serve avodah zarah is not the product of training, as with soldiers or terrorists, but a G-dly instinct, like an animal giving itself for its young without any reasoning.
Fear of Hashem is a product of love: like a mother who holds her baby tightly on the stairs because she loves it, a Jew fears that his love should not be damaged.

From the Avnei Nezer the Mashgiach draws that the bond between a Jew and Hashem is a felt intuition: a kohenes, from Shevet Levi who feel that bond more strongly, should have sensed that her husband was alive despite one witness.
'Ein maspikin beyado' does not lock the door of teshuvah: it only means no heavenly arousal is sent, but one who pushes his way in with his elbows is still helped.

Above, there is no 'temporary': since Heaven is beyond time, an aveirah is stamped into eternity, and the teshuvah that undoes it is likewise eternal; this is why the soul refuses even a temporary separation.
Chanukah, just before Shovevim, prepares for the darkest season; today the menorah is lit inside because the darkness has already penetrated our homes through the media.
'Ki karov' is explained through a reckoning: a Jew who would give his whole life against idolatry can surely give up the 'smaller nefesh' of a single desire, since nefesh also means desire.
Refraining from an aveirah for a few minutes is not a passing act; since nothing is temporary above, that moment's union with Hashem is eternal.
In holiness 'one' is the biggest number: if a person or even a table exists alongside Hashem, there are already two, so 'Echad' demands that the self be merged into Him.
The Torah never changes; where it seems to take another form for us, it is like a cloud that changes shape yet stays the same cloud.
The difficulty in grasping the eternity of a mitzvah is not in the logic but in a mind molded by this world, which takes the 'world of imagination' for the world of truth.
Teshuvah for a prohibition may bring forgiveness yet leave damage, like a host who forgives the guest who broke his bottle of wine while the bottle still must be replaced.
'Achta v'ashuv' applies only when the expected teshuvah is what allows the sin; one who sincerely regrets but fears his weak nature will fail again is forgiven each time.

Physical strength does not decide a wrestling match, energy does: an ox is stronger than a lion yet loses, and so too a person with greater spiritual strength loses to the yetzer hara if he is heavy with sadness.
Sadness is not only a weakness but a cause of sin: deprived of happiness, a person reaches for gratification, as an unhappy person reaches for another slice of cake.
The advantage the passuk finds in sorrow is not in the sadness itself but in its product, teshuvah, and the simcha after it is like the joy of two close friends who reconcile after a quarrel.
In its deepest sense, mourning the churban at Tikkun Chatzos is mourning one's own private Beis HaMikdash, which a person ruined through his aveiros.
Suffering comes from the higher, hidden half of the Shem Havayah; it is a closer contact with Hashem that a person is not yet conditioned to receive, so it arrives as pain.
The Alter Rebbe's power, which made him a target, was that he immunized his chassidim against anything this world has to offer, and that power is contained in the words of this chapter.
Complaining that one's situation is bad shows self-love: such a person wants to step out from under Hashem's hand, which is running his affairs the way Hashem knows is best for him.
The letter opens with 'Lehaskil HaBinah' because the root of the chasadim is in Binah, and gevuros raised to Binah are sweetened at their root.
Pharaoh, after the plague of locusts, sensed something drawn from the fiftieth gate of Binah: he saw blood ahead of Klal Yisroel, but not that it would turn into the blood of milah.
Remorse over aveiros is 'by appointment only'; for a real rasha sadness can strike anytime, since he has no program and no appointments.
The higher a person rises, the more a small stain of sin becomes significant, like a stain on a coat that is unimportant for a delivery boy but intolerable before an audience with a king.
Making up the sukkah meal on Shemini Atzeres means, in the Chassidish explanation, that the sukkah escorts a Jew into the house.
The Ba'al Shem Tov's new path was not to reveal more secrets but to take the secrets of the Zohar and the Arizal and use them for avodas Hashem, which is why spreading them in his way is a mitzvah.
The Meor Einayim allowed only the teachings he did not remember saying to be printed, since a teaching he could not recall had been said from a far higher state.

Because the Tanya builds its concepts step by step from the beginning, it supplies the foundations that the other chassidic sefarim assume, so one who learns it can understand the Meor Einayim and the Kedushas Levi.
Reb Meir Arik held that one does not truly know hilchos Chanukah, since there is no Shulchan Aruch HaRav on those halachos, only the Shulchan Aruch with its commentaries.
The chassidim explained that the Ba'al HaTanya wanted the boat stopped by the boatmen rather than by his own miracle, because a mitzvah should be done in the natural way.

The Mashgiach suggests that the four letters of 'Tanya' are the four prefixes of the Hebrew future tense, so the very name of the sefer speaks of wanting to become: what was until now is past, and from now on one wants to be good.
Shevuah comes from sheva: since all the forces of creation lie in the seven days, an oath binds a person with the strength of all of creation, and that is why it helps against the yetzer hara.

'Mashbi'in oso' can be read as 'mashpi'in': pei and beis interchange, and in ksav ashuri a pei holds a white beis inside it, so the oath is a flow of holiness sent down from heaven to enable the soul to fulfill it.
Being 'like a rasha' in one's own eyes does not mean thinking oneself a rasha; it means not being sure of oneself.
According to the Raya Mehemna, the 'bad' and 'good' in the Gemara's four types are not what happens to a person but the yetzer within him and who is master over whom.

Unlike most chassidish sefarim, which teach on the parsha without a set progression, the Tanya proceeds systematically from easy matters to higher ones, laying down knowledge before giving guidance in avodah.
Having bad thoughts in davening is not evidence of a bad soul: it would be, the Mashgiach says, only if a person had just one soul; since there are two, the struggle itself is expected.
The soul left a carefree heaven where it sang with the angels; it was sent down precisely to fight, so the war is the purpose, not a failure.

The walnut's structure, three inedible shells and a fourth brown skin eaten with the nut around four sections, mirrors the three impure kelipos, nogah, and the four letters of Hashem's Name in the soul.
Nogah is like sunlight filtered through a window shade: there is some light, but not real light, which is why it can go either way.
Salt, melach, has the same letters as bread, lechem, and the Mashgiach connects it to three times Hashem's Name, which is why one dips the bread in salt three times.
The same body that is a barrier to the soul can be elevated: the Jew's yetzer comes from nogah, and how he eats decides whether it turns to holiness or to impurity.
The Mashgiach explains that the nations kept customs from Noach whose reasons they forgot: red for stop and green for go reflect blood as gevurah and green as life.
Doctors and bakers wear white, an impractical color, because they bestow chesed; their mazal sees what they themselves do not know.
Water has no taste, color or smell, yet people drink it with relish, because water itself is pleasure and all pleasures come from it.
Anger is a form of pride: a person who has worked on his pride will never get angry, since he does not demand that everything go as he wants.
When a tzaddik speaks simple words, even jests or talk of politics, they can contain great yichudim through gematrios and initials.
Earth is the element that can never be nullified and always sinks downward; from it come sadness and laziness, a life without energy or will.
Each bad middah behaves like its element: pride rises like fire against the pull that brings everything else down, while sadness lies down like earth, which falls fastest.
Wild music belongs to the element of air: it has no substance and makes a person ownerless, bound to nothing, like the Gemara's slave who prefers hefker.
Kelipas nogah is like a window shade: a barrier between man and Hashem through which the sun still shines.
Orlah and bris milah share one pattern: three parts that cannot be redeemed and a fourth that is raised to holiness, matching the three impure kelipos and kelipas nogah.
Even a gentile's mercy can be selfish: he gives to the hungry so that he himself can enjoy his ice cream in peace.
The Mashgiach reads the Ramban's forty lashes together with the Gemara's thirty-nine: of the forty days of formation, the first point, the G-dly soul, never sinned, so it is not punished.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur form the year like the forty days of a child, and Yom Kippur corresponds to the untouched point of G-dliness, which is why one does not eat on it.
The Mashgiach notes that 'rotzeh ani' equals Yom Kippur in gematria: the point that says 'I want to serve Hashem' is the point revealed on that day.

Since Hashem blew the soul into Adam on Rosh Hashanah and renews creation each year, on Rosh Hashanah a Jew blows the shofar with great force from within, giving his soul back with teshuvah, which is why the one blowing turns red.
A person cannot understand Hashem not because he is not smart enough; even a billion times more intelligence or a million senses would not help, just as eyes cannot hear a niggun.
Tanya's distinction is its form: the same foundations found scattered in the sefarim of the Maggid's other disciples are laid out in it as one continuous sequence, like a textbook.
The Mashgiach reads 'ki karov' against its plain sense: yiras Shamayim is very hard, and it becomes near only for one who takes the long road, as in the Gemara's 'long-and-short' way.
The four letters of 'Tanya' are exactly the letters that form the future tense in loshon hakodesh, so the word itself speaks of 'I will be', the stance of one doing teshuvah.
Avraham's oath was not a sign of distrust in Eliezer but a provision for an emergency: an oath unlocks reserves a person cannot reach on his own.
Shevuah is tied to sheva (seven), sova (satiation) and shefa (flow), since beis and peh interchange; the Mashgiach notes that the peh in a sefer Torah holds a white beis within it.
The oath given to the soul before birth works like Shabbos for the weekday traveler: a recharge of strength drawn from a higher place for a hard journey.
The Ra'aya Mehemna reads tzaddik v'ra lo not as a tzaddik who suffers but as a tzaddik whose evil belongs to him: it is inside him, yet he is its master, like a man leading a dog on a leash.
The angel cannot announce tzaddik or rasha because, unlike Hashem's knowledge, a decree spoken through an angel or written in the Torah would compel the outcome and take away free choice.
'Mazal' comes from flowing down, like 'nozlim': it is the channel through which a person's physical bounty descends from above, and 'gad', said at Gad's birth, means mazal for the same reason.
Rabbah, a man of truth who never interrupted his learning, could not have called himself a beinoni if a beinoni sometimes sins; this forces the definition that a beinoni never sins at all.
'Chalal' in Dovid's verse carries both meanings, empty and slain: he slew his yetzer hara through fasting, and so his heart was left empty of it.
Great tzaddikim can remember their earlier gilgulim because they have no free choice to lose; ordinary people do not remember, because such memory would make it impossible for them to sin.
Just as Hashem creates some tzaddikim complete, He also has reshaim born to be wicked, because He needs them to carry out His plan for creation.

Beyond guarding the fruit, the klipah is called a shell because it is a barrier that must be cracked to reach the fruit, and breaking it, like getting past the keruvim guarding Gan Eden, is the purpose of a person's life.

The Kotzker read 'eishes chayil' as either the Torah, to which a talmid chacham is wedded, or a physical wife: a person cannot dance at both weddings, just as one cannot stand on both sides of the fence of the sitra achra.
In the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable the walls were never real; so too, the tzaddik who breaks through finds at the end that the klipah that looked like a mountain was no more than a hair.

Eating meat makes it part of a person, but blood is the vessel of the animal's own animal soul, so eating it would strengthen his own animal soul; this, the Mashgiach says, is why Hashem does not want it eaten.

Even the klipos come from Hashem's four-letter Name, so there are four of them, parallel to the four elements; the four coverings of a walnut picture them, with the thin skin eaten together with the nut standing for klipas nogah, which can become part of holiness.
Klipas nogah is like a translucent curtain on a window: one does not see the sun clearly, but its light comes through, unlike the other klipos, which make only darkness.

The four verbs of the Nusach Ari brachah against the wicked match the four kelipos: three call for uprooting and breaking, the impure kelipos, while the last, subduing, fits nogah, which is not destroyed but turned to the good.
Milah and periah mirror the kelipos: the layers cut away entirely are the three impure kelipos, while periah, which is not cut off but drawn back upward, is kelipas nogah turned toward the holy.

A goy's charity differs from a Jew's tzedakah not in the act but in its root: it is the animal kindness even predators show their young, exercised to satisfy oneself, while a Jew's mercy, even without conscious intent, comes from the side of kedushah.
Fire's root is in the moon, which is why fire rises and burns better at night, under the moon's rule; the Mashgiach gives this as the reason the poskim require bedikas chametz at night.
Mockery is rooted in emptiness: a joke amuses in proportion to how far its statement is from reality, which is why leitzanus belongs to the element of air.
Sadness is a cousin of pride: it comes from a person feeling he ought to be something and is not, while true bitterness, like bitter herbs that stimulate the appetite, drives him to learn and daven.

The difference between olah and shelamim reflects the two kinds of animal soul: a goy can sacrifice something wholly to Hashem, but only a Jew can make his eating itself part of the offering, since only his animal soul, from nogah, can be turned to kedushah.

Intellect fails to grasp Hashem not because it is too weak but because it is the wrong sense, as ears cannot paint a picture, and a watch cannot understand the watchmaker; even a 'billion IQ' would not help.
The halachos are like a lead container around radioactive material: the garment is what lets a person hold Hashem's very presence in his mind and hands without being harmed.
Because the holiness is so great, it needs the coarsest garments, so the most worldly halachos, such as the laws of damages and of plotting witnesses, hold the highest light.
The laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah are all found in the sedras read during Sefirah, because purity and holiness of the middos are the foundation for receiving the Torah.
The passuk says 'pihu' rather than 'piv' because 'peh' and 'fah' join into one word, showing a union so strong that the two became one, as when a Jew learns Torah.

Hashem's 'right hand' embracing the person means the Torah, which comes from chesed and water, the right side, as the first of the seven voices of Kabbalas Shabbos is 'the voice of Hashem upon the waters'.

The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah of the four kinds of students as a warning to those who visit many rebbes and pick out precisely what is not to be imitated, such as a tzaddik's eating, sleeping or anger, whose hidden reasons they do not see.

Different customs about dress while learning come from the climate where each group's rebbes lived; each follows how his rebbe behaved in his place, while the shared principle is derech eretz for Torah.

Torah has two aspects: as a vessel it draws G-dliness only when learned properly, but in itself it always keeps some holiness, like a dead body that still bears a trace of the soul, which is why people pray at the graves of tzaddikim.

The price of an esrog shows that G-dliness is clothed in it: no thought can grasp Hashem, yet one holding the lulav and esrog holds G-dliness in his hand and spreads it to all sides of the world when he shakes them.

Although the secrets of the Torah are higher because they have fewer garments, a Gemara or halacha understood clearly gives a stronger unity, since even angels cannot fully grasp sod, while a physical halacha can be truly understood.
R' Pinchas of Koretz explains that mitzvos cost money and Torah is free because Torah is bread, a basic necessity whose price is low, while mitzvos are garments, which are expensive.
The imprint of permitted pleasure is like a stain that remains after washing: even teshuvah removes the kelipas noga, but the trace needs a stronger 'detergent', chibut hakever.
The two Gehinoms match two failures: fire for one who warmed himself to an active sin, snow for the coldness and laziness of neglecting a positive mitzvah.
Idle chatter is a drive of the middos that even animals share, barking and singing; secular wisdom is worse precisely because its impurity reaches the higher level of chabad.
Torah and secular wisdom are opposites: Torah must be learned lishmah and not as a spade, while secular wisdom may be learned only as a spade and never for its own sake.
The wisdom of the nations rises and falls opposite the sages of Torah, as zeh l'umas zeh; when the Torah's sages are gone, the nations' wise men also decline.
An aveirah cannot be done lishmah, so a good intention cannot permit studies that require learning heresy, which comes from the three impure kelipos rather than kelipas noga.
The verse about Pharaoh says his heart was 'turned over', not merely bent: in the rasha gamur the good itself has become evil, the mirror image of the tzaddik gamur.
Tzaddikim gemurim could remember their earlier gilgulim because they have no bechirah left to lose; others are not given that memory, since remembering would take away their bechirah.
Love of Hashem and hatred of evil are measured against each other: whoever does not hate evil completely cannot love Hashem completely, except in elevated moments of davening.
Like the fragrance of a korban that rises up, the bnei aliyah take the evil itself and raise it to such a level that it ascends to Heaven, where no evil can exist.
The greatest tzaddikim serve Hashem not even to quench their own thirst for Him, but to do kindness with the Shechinah in exile, like a son toiling to redeem his parents.
The brain, though the seat of the Godly soul, is driven by the heart: the blood the heart sends up activates the brain to devise ways of fulfilling the heart's wishes.
Following the Midrash, Pharaoh's 'heavy heart' means his heart was a liver, all blood: he could admit his sin but had no heart to fear Hashem and send the people out.

The order of the morning blessings embodies the Tanya's teaching: Birchas Yotzer's contemplation of the luminaries and the angels gives birth to the love of Ahavah Rabbah, as intellect gives birth to emotion.

Eating matzah with appetite is 'stealing' the yetzer hara's drive for the mitzvah; without it the mitzvah would lack its fire and completeness, which is the meaning of serving 'with both your inclinations'.
Beyond 'avodas avodah', service by toil, there is 'avodas matanah', a gifted delight in serving Hashem that even a simple person can be granted at high moments.
Subduing the yetzer hara is like a conquering king who has not made the defeated king his friend but holds him as a prisoner, and this every Jew can achieve.
The yetzer hara's own joy, like the harlot in the Zohar's parable, is that the person not be seduced, so that even the yetzer hara is subservient to Hashem.

The Mashgiach explains that a sinful thought is 'light' only in how easily one falls into it; in its damage it is graver than a deed, because a deed blemishes Asiyah while a thought reaches Beriah, up to the Throne of Glory.

He maps the three garments onto the worlds: a good deed illuminates the world of Asiyah, a good word the higher world of Yetzirah, corresponding to ruach, and a good thought the world of Beriah; their opposites blemish those same worlds.

Even the rasha v'ra lo is not cut off: the good he drove out stays around him as a makif, as if standing at the door asking to be let back in, which is why he would still give his life rather than serve idols.
When ten Jews gather, their souls merge into one and draw down a holiness that nine tzaddikim cannot, which is why the surrounding kedushah of even a rasha v'ra lo allows him to complete the ten.

The Ba'al HaTanya called his work a book for beinonim because becoming a tzaddik cannot be taught; one must be born for it. But refusing ever to obey the yetzer hara is in every Jew's hands, so every Jew can be a beinoni.

'Never sinned and never will' does not mean literally never; it is like a report card on his present state: one who sinned and did complete teshuvah can be a beinoni, and even great people who later fell were judged by the level they stood on.

The beinoni is like a court where two judges sit: the evil judge may voice his opinion, but the beinoni listens only to the judge seated in the right chamber of the heart; during proper davening the evil one may not even speak.

The Mashgiach distinguishes between being judged a tzaddik and being a tzaddik as a title: on the day of judgment the beinoni will be called a tzaddik because he never sinned, but by definition he is not one, since the desire for evil remains.

Foreign thoughts during davening are explained as the keruvim and the flaming sword at the gates of the heavenly chambers pushing out one who is not worthy to enter; the soul feels being thrown out, and the body feels it as stray thoughts.
The Gemara's three names of the yetzer, passer-by, guest and master, describe the stages of letting it in; the beinoni keeps it a passer-by at the door and never lets it sit down in his house.

Against those who say darkness is only an absence, the Mashgiach holds that spiritually darkness is a creation; that a little light nevertheless drives away much darkness shows the inherent dominion of light, and likewise of holy thought over the folly of the kelipah.
When the yetzer sees it cannot get a servant of Hashem to sin, it tries to make him feel important after a good davening, and that thought alone can cause the davening to be rejected.

The Mashgiach reads Yosef's kindness to his brothers as emunah: since the suffering had to come from somewhere, Yosef preferred that it come through holy tzaddikim, and he even owed them thanks for the atonement it brought.
Among created forces good and evil are always in balance, but the Creator of both light and darkness stands above that balance and joins the side of good, so the one on the side of good must win.
Spiritual darkness is a real entity, not merely the absence of light, yet it flees completely from light because light is Hashem's life-giving power, which nothing can neutralize.
Following the Maggid Meisharim, the tzaddik receives full credit at the judgment even though Hashem helped him, because he had the choice to be bad and chose good.

One who learns Torah lishmah all day is in a constant state like Krias Shema and tefillah, so he may never feel a desire for sin, yet his yetzer is only asleep; this is how Rabbah could think he was a beinoni.

The Mashgiach defines truth by permanence: worldly pleasure is like a 'chalal', one slain, empty of content, and leaves a void, while joy in a Yom Tov, a mitzvah or a blatt Gemara remains even afterward.

Yisrael begins with the letters that make it 'li rosh', a head, and Yaakov is 'akev', the heel, with the small yud as its point; so Yaakov binds all Jews from the highest to the lowest, who has nothing but the point of a Jew.
Because each board of the Mishkan is a level of Jews and Yaakov's attribute of truth passes through all of them, the same service can be falsehood for a higher person and truth for a lower one.
Following the Yismach Moshe, for a great servant of Hashem 'vachai bahem' means the life of the soul in Torah, so for him losing a mitzvah is death, and he may give his life for it.
For the beinoni, 'sfas emes tikon la'ad' means a truth that is packed away and waits for the next prayer, when with true preparation he can again keep the yetzer hara from disturbing him.

Without a bad thought the beinoni could not fulfil 'lo sasuru', so its coming is a chance for one of the Torah's greatest mitzvos, and pushing out a thought of idolatry breaks the root of the sitra achra.
The beinoni has 'ahavah betaanugim' only at moments, so when it is absent the desire for this world fills the place, since there is no vacuum.

The Mashgiach reads 'oved' as present tense: the beinoni is called an oved because his service is an unfinished, ongoing war, whereas for the tzaddik 'oved Hashem' is a name, like the title 'chacham'.
Like a swimmer on vacation whose exertion is pleasure, one who feels the sweetness of avodah experiences long nights of learning as recreation, not toil; but not everyone merits this at all times.
Avraham Avinu's work on himself changed his very creation into a new kind of being, one who believes in Hashem; creation was completed only with him, and from him comes every Jew's hidden love.
One who made himself a masmid through effort was an oved during the struggle, but once it became second nature he is 'lo avado', living off the dividends of his earlier toil.

Forgetting comes from the sitra achra, whose root Samech-Mem equals 100; reviewing 100 times breaks its power, and the 101st time, beyond habit, brings one into the realm of Michael, whose name equals 101.
The donkey drivers charge double for going just past their limit because it is beyond their regular routine; so too, going even slightly beyond one's habit is the hardest and most valuable step.
The oath's two halves are not of equal weight: 'do not be a rasha' is fully in a person's hands, while 'be a tzaddik' is a charge to strive, since being a tzaddik is not given to free choice.

Truth is measured by the person's level: a passing feeling of loathing for worldly pleasure is not truth for a complete tzaddik, but for the beinoni it is his truth, since he can renew it tomorrow at davening or next Shabbos.

Dovid's harp played at midnight like a piano string vibrating in response to a tuning fork: Dovid's heart was tuned to the song of the tzaddikim in Gan Eden, so it awoke by itself, with no alarm clock.
An ibbur benefits both souls: the Jew can serve with a love and joy beyond his own level, and the departed tzaddik gets to do once more the mitzvah he longed for or was missing.
Haman's ten thousand talents of charity lost to the barley omer because a non-Jew's deed stays below, while a Jew's cheapest offering is lifted (tenufah) and multiplied in the upper worlds.
'Aseres' denotes a collective and multiplication while 'isaron' denotes division, as 'ishon' (the pupil) means a small person reflected in the eye.

The Mashgiach reads King David's request to 'visit in His palace' as the plea of one who cannot always feel Hashem's sweetness to be at least an occasional guest, which Hashem grants every Jew at times of favor such as Shabbos and Yom Tov.
The Mashgiach applies 'a daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so' to every giver and receiver, so that Hashem matches each talmid to the rebbe with whom his soul stood at Sinai.

Counting by 'names' rather than numbers shows that each Jew is an individual letter with its own place in the Torah, which is why Moshe and the Nesi'im, who knew what lies in each Jew, had to do the counting.

Gerim are the crowns on the Torah's letters: not letters themselves but attached to them, which is why Rabbi Akiva, from a family of gerim, expounded the crowns, while Moshe Rabbeinu, the root of the letters themselves, did not grasp his teaching.

The Gemara's rule that each line of a Sefer Torah holds thirty letters so 'lemishpechoseichem' fits three times hints that the Torah's letters are arranged in families, as Jewish souls are born into the family where their letter belongs.

The Mashgiach maps the dispute onto the sefiros: Chabad spoke of the higher faculties, chochmah, binah and da'as, while the other chassidim emphasized the middos, love, fear and tiferes, and each follows his root.

Following the Yismach Moshe, the Mashgiach explains that 'vachai bahem' means biological life for a simple person but spiritual life for a great one, so the same Torah demands different things according to each person's level, just as 'very near' does.

Spiritual life, like the heart's beat, is a pulse rather than a steady flow: every person must go up and fall back, and this explains how the Yismach Moshe could taste the Rambam's fear from a moment of katnus.
The tzaddikim felt intense love and fear because their pure souls had no 'insulation': like an electric current, it passes through only where nothing blocks it.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, the mountain held over Klal Yisrael at Sinai was not for that fiery generation but for later generations, who would have to force themselves to learn and serve.

Chazal chose the word 'metzarfah', joins, rather than 'it is as if he did it' as a second intention: it hints that Hashem joins the intellectual love of the mind to the physical deed, which by nature cannot be joined.

The order of davening follows Tanya's path: korbanos and ketores clear away the kelipos, birchos krias shema contemplate the greatness of creation and the angels, and only then can one say ahavah rabbah and accept the yoke of Heaven in Shema.
Reb Zusha took the peasant's words about the hay, 'you can but you do not want to', as a rebuke to himself, since raising the fallen hei is the avodah of Jews in exile.

On the level of remez, 'galu le'Edom' means Jews fell to the conduct of Edom, and the inner exile draws the outer one; the Shechinah in exile is the spark of G-dliness in a Jew held captive by his kelipah.

Avraham's tenth trial was not the self-sacrifice of the akeidah, since he had already let himself be thrown into the furnace on the strength of his mind alone, but the closing of his heart, seeing Hashem 'from afar'.
The meraglim's trial was the same as Avraham's tenth: their lack of feeling in Eretz Yisrael was a shell to be broken like a nut, not a sign against the land.
Tamuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, and as months given over to the sitra achra they are the time to break it with a broken spirit.
Atzvus and atzlus (sadness and laziness) are the same thing at root: both come from the element of earth, the heaviest element, which is why a sad person has no drive to fight the yetzer hara.
The Tanya's 'at set times' is like a doctor's sign 'by appointment only': sadness over sins may come in only at its appointed time, never as a guest with its own key.
Following the method of related sounds, simcha is linked to leaning on someone and atzvus to being forsaken; idols are called atzabim because one who relies on them has nothing to lean on.
Mourning the Beis HaMikdash at Tikkun Chatzos means, inwardly, mourning the mikdash in each Jew's heart that was ruined by his sins, which is regret over them.
Suffering is like a costly wine such as port: it comes from a very high world, but it tastes bitter to one who is not a connoisseur, as the finest brandy tastes bitter to a child.

Atzvus pushes a person into taavos, because he cannot bear being dissatisfied and looks for some satisfaction, such as a piece of cake; this is why the yetzer hara brings on sadness in the middle of one's work.

The hidden love is not a feeling a Jew develops, but part of his very being, like the inherited instincts of animals: an ox craves grass and a lion meat because its parents did, not because it cultivated the desire.

Yaakov's shepherding of Lavan's flocks was the freeing of Jewish souls from the sitra achra; the Midrash's 600,000 sheep are the 600,000 souls, and the opinion of 600,000 flocks reflects that a whole group of Jews belongs to each letter of the Torah.
Every tzaddik has a counterpart in kelipah of matching strength, and when the tzaddik leaves the world his counterpart falls too; therefore Nimrod was killed the very day Avraham died.

Leah is the hidden aspect of the Shechinah and Rachel the revealed one; the hidden love in every Jew is the aspect of Leah, buried deep like Leah in the Me'aras HaMachpelah, and the avodah is to bring it to the revealed aspect of Rachel.

As blond hair hidden in a dark-haired father can appear again in his son, so the great soul-powers hidden in a simple Jew can be revealed in his child; this is how a simple Jew can father a great tzaddik.
Hashem sometimes has a very lofty soul born to an unlikely parent, as Avraham to Terach and David in a hidden way, so that the Satan will not foresee it and interfere until it is too late.
A Jew who guards his eyes makes them a merkavah: two times 'ayin' equals 260, ten times the Name of Hashem, which the Mashgiach connects to 'ki sar liros' said of Moshe.

Through the Avnei Nezer, the Mashgiach reads the penalty of a bas Levi who remarried on false testimony as a demand of sensitivity: her tribe stayed bound to Hashem at the Egel, so she should have felt that her husband was alive.

From the Lechovitcher the Mashgiach shows that a talmid truly bound to his rebbe feels the bond, and his distress comes from not knowing why it is gone; once the reason is known, the feeling is natural and there is nothing to lament.
Following the Kotzker, the Targum's 'to the side of' a woman shows that love of this world and love of Torah are two sides of one fence: a person can stand on either, never on both.

Losing one's bechirah is itself a punishment for not using it earlier, which the Mashgiach applies to Pharaoh: his hardened heart at the plagues was the penalty for oppressing the Jews while he still had choice.

The Mashgiach connects teshuvah tata'ah with the four species as the letters of Hashem's Name: the esrog is the last heh, and holding it apart from the lulav, as in the Rokeach's dream, is a separated heh that teshuvah reunites.
As long as the heh is apart from the Name, the forces of the sitra achra stay joined, like Rome that is full while Yerushalayim is ruined; teshuvah reverses it, so the sitra achra splits apart.

Chochmah is not cleverness but the 'koach mah', the unexplained first flash that a person receives as if from heaven and then builds out with binah, which is why the Chovos HaLevavos calls it close to prophecy.
Not grasping Hashem is not a weakness of the mind: the mind is simply not the organ for it, just as no improvement of eyesight would let a person see music.

'Pesi ya'amin lechol davar' is a quality, not a lack: before Hashem everyone is a 'pesi', and Dovid HaMelech's admission that he was like a beast before Hashem is itself what keeps him always with Him.

The proof that Jewish mesirus nefesh comes from the soul's root is that those who gave their lives were never indoctrinated and often did not even understand the Shema they cried out, unlike soldiers who are trained to die.
In loshon hakodesh, 'emunah' joins belief and faithfulness in one word, and so it works both ways: Hashem believes in and is faithful to the Jews just as they believe in Him.
'Mah titzak elai' hints that the rescue of Klal Yisrael as a whole does not depend on tefillah, since the nation is bound to Hashem at its root in atika.
Tu Bishvat is the yom tov of emunah: like a tree whose sap begins to rise in its roots while it still looks dead under the snow, emunah lives at the root, and so Parshas Beshalach is read around it.

The difference between Jewish and gentile self-sacrifice: gentiles die for falsehood only after being brainwashed, while Jews who were never trained give their lives because the soul's root in chochmah acts like an instinct.
A Jew sways in davening and learning because his soul, like a flame, pulls upward; the Mashgiach ties this to the story of identifying a Jewish child by who sways over the Gemara.
Teva is a 'borrowed name' for the point where explanation ends; calling the soul's longing teva means it is rooted above reason.
Purim belongs to the lowest Jews: Adar is the lowest of the months and Adar Sheni lower still, and the drinking of 'ad delo yada' reveals what lies above daas even in the emptiest Jew.
The 'Canaani' is called a merchant because kelipah's kindness is circular: the merchant gives only so that it comes back to him, while holy chesed goes out to give.
In the sitra achra the order is reversed: the female is stronger than the male, and the Mashgiach connects this to the gentile custom of 'ladies first'.
The Mashgiach treats the sinner's readiness for martyrdom and his daily sinning as the same human folly, illustrated by the smoker who would refuse to be shot yet keeps smoking.
Only man can choose to act against his own survival; no animal ever does, which shows that sin is folly rather than strong desire.
Adar, from the word for a covering cloak, is the month of hidden miracles, just as the hidden love belongs to Jews whose faith is covered; Adar Sheni is further still from Nissan.
Purim is above all the festival of the simple and the sinful, and the drinking of Purim reveals the hidden love that lies above reason.
The merit for the Jews who bowed to the image in Haman's time is that in their hearts they never denied Hashem, which comes out on Purim.

The Mashgiach reads a puzzling Tosafos through the Tzemach Tzedek: the tzaddik who later gave his life al kiddush Hashem was a Jew who had not transgressed in this matter, since one who had would not have had the strength for mesiras nefesh.

Gentile self-sacrifice comes from daily drilling, like soldiers trained to die for the king, while Jews, even the lowest, have given their lives in hundreds of thousands out of an inner instinct that would not let them be torn from Hashem.

The donkey knows its master only through the feeding trough, whereas the ox knows its owner directly; a Jew who does not sense Hashem has numbed this instinct through sin, like a dentist's anesthetic.
A person's soul extends into his possessions; this explains why the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair would not eat untithed food and why a Canaanite slave may eat terumah.
Among created things one is the smallest number, since anything can be halved; with Hashem 'echad' is the greatest number, a oneness without limit after which there is no other.

A person thinks in a language, usually his mother tongue, yet the first stirring, like hunger, comes from the essence of the soul before any letters; an animal has the desire but no letters of thought.
The Mashgiach reads Shlomo HaMelech's 'three thousand meshalim' as a chain: a mashal on a mashal on a mashal, down three thousand levels, until a very deep matter could be understood.
According to the Mashgiach, the good tastes of this world exist so that a person should grasp, through them, the sweetness of Torah, which is called sweeter than honey.
The Mashgiach compares a Jew washing his hands in the morning to a power station that lights a whole city: he purifies his share of creation from the defect of the night.

The Mashgiach uses the law that one sitting on layers above a zav's seat becomes tamei without touching it to show that a mitzvah makes a person a merkavah, not merely someone in contact with holiness.
The Mashgiach explains that sins work like an anesthetic: they dull a person's senses so that he does not feel that learning Gemara unites him with Hashem.
Not feeling the holiness of Torah study is itself a protection, the Mashgiach says: a person who felt the light he unites with while learning would be consumed by it.
The Arizal's emphasis on tefillah before Moshiach is like a doctor ordering orange juice for a sick man: bread and meat remain the main food, but in his condition he now needs the juice.

There are two kinds of yirah: a lower one that makes a person sit down to learn, and a higher one that comes from the learning itself; relative to that higher yirah Torah is the gate, which settles the Gemara's seemingly contradictory statements.

Not feeling yirah while learning is like surgery under anesthesia: the patient feels nothing, yet the operation is truly taking place; the soul and its root feel the bond with Hashem even when the body does not.

Rabbinic laws are Hashem's own wisdom: He left them for the sages of each generation to enact at the right time with divine inspiration, and according to the Arizal they come from a higher root, which is why the second day of Yom Tov is on a higher level.
The Satan himself, like Bilaam who could not go against Hashem's word, does whatever Hashem wants; only a sinning Jew acts against Hashem's will, which is why he is worse than the sitra achra.

The goat to Azazel, the hair showing at the tefillin, kaparos, the thirty-nine lashes and the ban on matzah on Erev Pesach all leave the sitra achra a small share, at Hashem's command, so that it is not wholly nullified before Moshiach.

The Magen Avraham's custom about kiddush is not fear of Maadim's harm, since all harsh forces flee from Shabbos; rather, making kiddush in that hour would take the red wine, Maadim's own, entirely into holiness and leave the sitra achra nothing.

Even the sitra achra and the angel at the head of the forces of impurity know that Hashem rules and submit to Him; the sinner, the only creature that rebels against His will, is therefore lower than them.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Mashgiach explains that sinning while knowing Hashem sees, as if He would let it pass, contains a spark of kefirah, even if one forgets it at the time.
Ordinary waste mixed with food still contains a little food, but the dregs of this world, its lusts and sins, are pure waste with no good at all.
A moment of sweetness in avodah is like a free sample Hashem gives to awaken a person; afterwards he must pay the full price with toil until he earns that sweetness himself.

A father in a rage at his child still snatches him from a speeding car, because his natural love, hidden under the anger, surfaces when the child's life is at stake; so too a Jew's hidden love surfaces when faced with idolatry.
The spirit of folly covers the soul only up to chochmah; idolatry touches chochmah itself, so there the hidden love wakes, while other sins slip past it.
Wild animals rule over a man only when he appears to them like a beast, having lost his tzelem Elokim through sin; one who keeps it cannot be harmed by them.
An improper thought arriving is not the sin; the sin is letting it remain in one's head, since a person is created with a body precisely to face such trials.

Because the Torah is eternal and addresses the smallest Jew as much as Moshe Rabbeinu, 'ki karov eilecha hadavar me'od' must be true for the smallest person too, which is why the Tanya needs a short way.
Talmud Torah is the hardest mitzvah because it claims every free moment and the full depth of understanding one is capable of.

The Gemara's ruling that one interrupts learning for the Megillah shows that bittul Torah exists even while learning: hearing the Megillah superficially is bittul compared to learning Gemara with full depth.
A shopkeeper who opens his store but serves customers half-heartedly is also guilty of idling from work; in the same way, learning below one's capacity is a form of bittul Torah.
The hidden love is like a father's love for a son he is angry at: concealed while the son sins, but revealed the moment the son is in danger.

The Mashgiach likens a Jew's emunah to the inherited instinct of animals: just as a young bee, beaver or spider builds what its parents built without being taught, a Jew believes in Hashem because it is in his system.

Reading 'behibaram' as 'b'Avraham', the Mashgiach says creation was not complete after 'Vayechulu': a new creature still had to be made, one who believes in Hashem by instinct, and the added hei, the letter of birth, makes that belief pass to his children.
A Jew who says he does not believe is usually deceiving himself to excuse his desires, a pattern the Mashgiach finds in Esav blaming his wives and in Chiel explaining away the deaths of his children.
Tevilah is a new birth through self-nullification: one bends like a curled-up fetus and comes out a new creation, which is why the Mashgiach says a shortcut of dipping a finger misses the point.
