The Mashgiach notes that a mashal holds in only one detail, and that the Avos as merkavah were more than a chariot: a chariot is nullified to its rider but not part of him, while the Avos were permeated with G-dliness in every limb.

Love and fear of Hashem are themselves the 'offspring' of chochmah and binah, father and mother, male and female, which is why the Tanya must explain how they can be included together in an inherited love.
Toward a person, love and fear pull against each other; only toward Hashem do they coexist, because loving Him means union and fearing Him means nullification, and both belong together.
Calling the avos a merkavah is a mashal that holds in one point only: a chariot stays a separate thing from its rider, while the avos became one with Hashem, a level of Elokus itself.
Acquired knowledge is not inherited, but what is part of a person's essence is; the avos' bond with Hashem had become their essence, which is why Jews inherit a hidden love.
Ruach and neshamah that a person never revealed still surround him as a makif connected to his inner self, so, like a hair color that skips a generation, they can appear in his children.
Vapor and ice are the same substance with a vast difference between them; so too the worlds are one light, ever more contracted and physical.
A child may be cleverer than an adult and still lack daas, since daas is not intelligence but the power to govern the midos.
The name Atzilus comes from 'etzel', near: like the nobles who stand beside the king and receive his light, Atzilus is the world closest to the Creator.
The four worlds with their ten sefiros are Hashem's reshus hayachid, ten handbreadths high and four wide, while what passes to the sitra achra is already the reshus harabim.

Like an aspirin under a sweet coating and an enteric coating, a Jew's outer garments differ, coarse for the simple Jew and refined for the talmid chacham, but what lies beneath is the same in every Jew.
Because holiness is unity and impurity is the 'world of division', a Jew can bind himself to the Avos only through unity with other Jews and the tzaddik.
In a round dance everyone stands at the same distance from the center, where Hashem is; by lifting a person above himself, dancing reveals the inner point in which all Jews are equal.
Machol and mechilah are one word: Yom Kippur brings forgiveness because on that day the inner point of every Jew, which does not want to be cut off from Hashem, is revealed.
Hashem calls the Jews 'bnei kushiyim' because, as with skin color, the difference he rebukes them for lies only in the outer layer, while beneath it all Jews are equal.
Spiritual greatness can be inherited hidden, like a physical trait or a talent for niggun that skips a generation and reappears in the grandson.
Hashem hides great souls in unlikely homes the way an owner hides diamonds where a thief would never think to look, so that the Satan, who guards the line of Moshiach, is outwitted.
Chanukah, set in Teves, the month given to Esav and the year's longest night, parallels ikvesa dimeshicha, the 'heel' of history, where Moshiach is revealed precisely in the deepest darkness.
The lower a generation has sunk, the higher its souls fell from: like a stone dropped from a roof that sinks deeper into mud, today's souls can reach sparks earlier generations could not.
An inventor can explain every part of his machine but not why the cement falls rather than rising; that given starting point, which binah builds on but cannot explain, is what is called chochmah.

In a pilpul on the Rambam everything can be explained except its starting point, which stands like a gezeirah; so too there is a power in a Jew that exists but cannot be understood, the Jewish neshamah inherited from the Avos.

Since emunah means believing what one does not understand, it does not depend on intellect at all; it comes from chochmah, which is above intellect, so the greatest talmid chacham's emunah is no more a product of his mind than that of the simplest Jew.

The Mashgiach reads David HaMelech's 'I was a beast before You' together with 'and I am always with You': because he knew he had no understanding before Hashem, he was always bound to Him through emunah.
A Jew's readiness to die for Hashem is like a hen's readiness to fight for her eggs: not reasoning but nature, because Hashem is the Jew's source as parents are the source of a child.

Chametz on Pesach and chalav akum are singled out because they tie a Jew to the goy; the Mashgiach connects this to Pesach itself, whose mitzvos begin with separating from avodah zarah, and to the passuk that puts the ban on molten idols next to keeping the festival of matzos.
